newsitem.title: UK: West plans fresh Balkan summit for December.
newsitem.headline: West plans fresh Balkan summit for December.

text.p: Faced with the need to keep NATO troops in Bosnia well into next year, Western powers plan to summon Balkan leaders and demand fresh commitments to peace after this week's elections, diplomats said on Monday.

A London summit, planned for December, will take place regardless of the outcome of Bosnia's first post-war elections on Saturday. Critics have said the elections will do little more than foster existing divisions in the country.

Diplomats said foreign ministers of key Western nations and Russia would attend the two-day meeting, along with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic.

They said the summit would take place after a NATO foreign ministers meeting in the first week of December, at which the alliance is expected to agree that some troops should remain in Bosnia next year to underpin the fragile peace.

"What people are looking for is a new set of commitments, looking forward into next year so that our continued presence is underpinned by commitments from the parties," said one Western diplomat, who asked not to be identified.
"We are having this meeting because it is obvious we need to keep the pressure on, whatever the results of the elections," said another envoy in a European capital.

Last November's Dayton peace agreement ended Europe's worst war in half a century but has done little to consolidate peace. There are problems with freedom of movement, the return of refugees, economic reconstruction and wider reconciliation.

Municipal elections have already been postponed and the new political structures for Bosnia, set out in the Dayton accord, are in trouble -- particularly the Moslem-Croat federation, a key pillar of the planned federal state.
International peace coordinator Carl Bildt warned on Monday that a refusal by nationalists to share power after Saturday's national elections would mean a new war.
"If we don't implement the constitution, we are lost, and so is peace," Bildt told a news conference in Sarajevo.
Diplomats said the London summit was not supposed to produce another Dayton-style treaty but was aimed rather at getting the key players to stick to their commitments.
Richard Holbrooke, the tough U.S. negotiator who brokered the Dayton peace deal, said last week such talks would be needed to prevent Bosnia from disintegrating under various pressures.

Western allies, including the United States, have privately accepted the need for a continued military presence in Bosnia next year, although the original plan was to withdraw the 60,000-strong peace force in December, after just one year.
Diplomats said the London summit would discuss the size and structure of any force left in Bosnia next year and ways of improving coordination between the civilian and military effort.
Foreign ministers from countries involved in Bosnia are also expected to discuss these issues at a meeting with Bildt in Paris, scheduled for November.

In the last few weeks some European allies have begun to acknowledge the need for a continued military presence in Bosnia openly, although the subject remains highly sensitive in the United States ahead of November's presidential elections.

Foreign ministers of the 15-nation European Union, meeting in Ireland at the weekend, endorsed the idea of a two-year civilian "peace consolidation" programme in Bosnia -- an idea first proposed by France.
"I think it is evident there is going to be a long-term engagement...both military and civilian," said Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring after the meeting.
